title: Unity Catalog Mastery
subtitle: Phase 3 — metastore → catalog → schema → object, grants, storage, volumes, policies and the PERMISSION_DENIED algorithm
mantra: Every Unity Catalog question is four questions — WHO? WHAT OBJECT? WHAT ACTION? WHERE ARE THE BYTES? — and every PERMISSION_DENIED is a walk down the whole authorization chain, not just "do I have SELECT?".
objectives: You can explain why Unity Catalog exists, what it stores (metadata, permissions, lineage, storage references) and what it does NOT store (the bytes).
You can place metastore, workspace, catalog, schema and object correctly and parse any `catalog.schema.object` name.
You can write real GRANT / REVOKE / SHOW GRANTS statements and predict the effect of USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, inheritance, ownership, MANAGE, ALL PRIVILEGES and BROWSE.
You can contrast managed vs external tables and volumes, including what DROP does to the files.
You can explain the chain cloud IAM → storage credential → external location → external table/volume → files, and managed storage locations.
You can protect data with row filters, column masks and ABAC, and use lineage for impact analysis and debugging.
You can design the grants of a production lakehouse (groups + service principals, least privilege).
You can debug any PERMISSION_DENIED with the 8-layer algorithm (I Bet Cats Sit On Fluffy Silk Cushions) and the six classic cases.

sections.title: The Four Questions & Why Unity Catalog Exists
sections.hook: Four questions explain almost all of Unity Catalog. Learn them first and the rest of the phase slots in around them.

blocks.text: The most important mental model of Phase 3: every governance question breaks into **four questions**, asked top to bottom.

WHO?            user / group / service principal
   │
   ▼
WHAT OBJECT?    metastore
                └── catalog
                    └── schema
                        ├── table     ├── view
                        ├── volume    ├── function
                        └── model
   │
   ▼
WHAT ACTION?    USE / SELECT / MODIFY / CREATE / READ VOLUME / ...
   │
   ▼
WHERE ARE       managed storage
THE BYTES?      or  external location → cloud object storage
blocks.caption: The Phase-3 mental model: WHO → WHAT OBJECT → WHAT ACTION → WHERE ARE THE BYTES

blocks.title: Make this one diagram clear
blocks.text: Once **WHO / WHAT OBJECT / WHAT ACTION / WHERE ARE THE BYTES** is clear, almost all of Unity Catalog starts to make sense. Every later section answers one of these four.
**Why does Unity Catalog exist?** Start without Databricks. A company keeps its data in **S3 / ADLS** folders and has **100 developers**.

S3 / ADLS
├── finance/
│   ├── payroll/
│   └── invoices/
├── sales/
│   ├── orders/
│   └── customers/
└── marketing/
blocks.caption: Just folders. Nothing here says who may read payroll.

blocks.text: Without **central governance** you must answer by hand:

items: Who can **read** payroll? Who can **write** orders?
Which **pipeline** created this table? Which **dashboard** uses this column?
What happens if someone reads the **storage path directly**, bypassing permissions?

blocks.label: Think first: what if permissions live only in the S3 bucket, Azure Storage, notebooks, clusters and BI tools?
blocks.text: You get **fragmented governance**: five places, five permission models, no single answer to "who has what?". Unity Catalog makes governance **central**.

Databricks describes Unity Catalog as a **hierarchical governance layer**: every governed asset is a **securable object**, privileges go to **users, groups or service principals**, the **metastore** is the top-level container, and assets live in the three-level namespace `catalog.schema.object`.

blocks.title: Unity Catalog ≠ storage
blocks.text: UC is **not** a giant database filesystem and does **not** store the Parquet bytes. It is **metadata + namespace + permissions + ownership + lineage + governance policies + storage references**. The bytes live in **S3 / ADLS / GCS**.

Unity Catalog
     │  governs
     ▼
table metadata
     │  points to / manages
     ▼
cloud storage  (S3 / ADLS / GCS)
blocks.caption: UC governs metadata that points at (or manages) cloud storage

blocks.title: Library catalogue + security desk
blocks.text: UC is the library's **catalogue and security desk**: it knows every book, who may borrow it and where it sits. The **books themselves** stand on shelves elsewhere — your cloud storage.

blocks.title: Recap → Chapter 1
blocks.text: Metadata ≠ data and UC ≠ Delta Lake were introduced in Chapter 1 ("Table Metadata & the Unity Catalog Namespace"). This chapter goes deep.

sections.title: Metastore, Workspace & the Hierarchy
sections.hook: The metastore sits above everything, and the workspace is not part of the namespace at all. Misplace either and your debugging goes wrong from the first step.

blocks.text: The hierarchy from the top: one **metastore** holds **catalogs**, catalogs hold **schemas**, schemas hold **objects**.

METASTORE
├── CATALOG: dev
│   ├── SCHEMA: bronze
│   ├── SCHEMA: silver
│   └── SCHEMA: gold
├── CATALOG: prod
│   ├── SCHEMA: bronze
│   ├── SCHEMA: silver
│   └── SCHEMA: gold
└── CATALOG: sandbox
blocks.caption: Metastore → catalogs → schemas

blocks.text:
prod
└── silver
    ├── orders            (table)
    ├── customers         (table)
    ├── products          (table)
    ├── files_volume      (volume)
    └── normalize_email() (function)
blocks.caption: Inside a schema: tables, volumes, functions …

blocks.text: Databricks treats the **catalog** as the **primary unit of data isolation**, and the **schema** as a finer organizational / access-control layer.
The **metastore** is the **top-level container of Unity Catalog for metadata and permissions**. It exposes the three-level namespace `catalog.schema.object`.

items.title: A metastore IS
points: metadata about catalogs, tables, volumes, external locations, credentials, shares, permissions …

blocks.text: Usually there is **one metastore per region**, and many workspaces in that region attach to it — so they share governance.

Databricks Account
├── Workspace A ──┐
├── Workspace B ──┼──►  Metastore Europe
└── Workspace C ──┘
blocks.caption: Many workspaces, one regional metastore → common governance

blocks.text: So two workspaces can see the **same governed object** when all three hold:

items: Both attached to the same metastore
blocks.caption: Three conditions for cross-workspace access

blocks.title: Metastore vs catalog
blocks.text: **Metastore** = top **regional** governance container. **Catalog** = primary **logical / data isolation** container **inside** the metastore. You do **not** create a metastore per project by default — isolation usually starts at the **catalog** level.

blocks.title: The workspace is not in the namespace
blocks.text: `catalog.schema.object` has no workspace level. A notebook **lives in** a workspace; `prod.sales.orders` is **registered in** the metastore. "Workspace above catalog" is wrong.

blocks.title: Recap → Chapter 4
blocks.text: Account vs workspace (one account, many workspaces, metastores configured at account level) is in Chapter 4, "Account vs Workspace".

sections.title: Catalogs, Schemas, Objects & Creating Them
sections.hook: Catalog = big boundary, schema = organization, object = the thing. Creating each already needs hierarchical privileges.

blocks.text:
prod . sales . orders
^^^^   ^^^^^   ^^^^^^
catalog schema object
blocks.caption: Three names, three levels

blocks.text: The **catalog** is the first level. Think of it as a large **logical / security boundary**.

head: Design style
Example catalogs
blocks.caption: There is no single right structure

blocks.text: Databricks recommends that catalogs represent **meaningful isolation boundaries** — environment, business unit, team or project — so that **hierarchical grants stay simple and logical**.
The **schema** is the second level: a child of a catalog that can contain **tables, views, volumes, models and functions**. Organize schemas by **layer, team, domain or use case**.
The third name is the **object**: table, view, volume, function, model, materialized view, streaming table … So the general form is **`catalog.schema.object`**, not always `catalog.schema.table`.

blocks.title: Recap → Chapter 4: fully qualified names
blocks.text: `SELECT * FROM prod.sales.orders` is **fully qualified**; `SELECT * FROM orders` depends on `current_catalog()` / `current_schema()` (set with `USE CATALOG` / `USE SCHEMA`). In production, fully qualified names are safer because they **remove ambiguity**. Details: Chapter 4, "Namespaces and Fully Qualified Names".

blocks.caption: Creating a catalog and a schema

head: You want to…
Privilege you typically need
rows: `USE CATALOG` **+** `CREATE SCHEMA` on the parent catalog `ecommerce`
blocks.caption: The first example that permissions are hierarchical

blocks.title: CREATE SCHEMA needs two privileges
blocks.text: `CREATE SCHEMA` alone is not enough: you also need `USE CATALOG` on the parent catalog. It is the first time you see that UC permissions are **hierarchical**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when CREATE CATALOG / CREATE SCHEMA fails
questions: Am I creating a catalog — then do I have CREATE CATALOG on the metastore?
Am I creating a schema — do I have BOTH USE CATALOG and CREATE SCHEMA on the parent catalog?
Am I using the fully qualified name, so the schema lands in the catalog I think?
Is the identity running this the one that holds the grants (me vs a job's service principal)?

sections.title: Securables, Principals, Groups & Service Principals
sections.hook: Grants connect a principal to a securable through a privilege. Grant to groups and run production as service principals, and an access list stays manageable.

blocks.title: Recap → Chapter 3
blocks.text: Principals (user / group / service principal), securables and the GRANT grammar were introduced in Chapter 3. New here: the full securable list, account-level provisioning, and why production **ownership and writes** belong to groups / service principals.

items.def: An object registered in Unity Catalog on which grants can be given to a principal: catalog, schema, table, volume, **external location, storage credential**, function …
An identity that receives permissions: **user** (`nikos@company.com`), **group** (`data_engineers`), **service principal** (`orders-etl-prod`).
An allowed **action** on a securable, e.g. `SELECT`, `MODIFY`, `USE SCHEMA`, `READ VOLUME`.

blocks.text: Databricks recommends provisioning principals at the **account level** and using **groups** instead of individual users wherever possible.

blocks.caption: Grant to groups, manage membership

blocks.text:
Maria joins the team
        │
        ▼
add Maria to group `analysts`
        │
        ▼
0 table grants changed  (not 200)
blocks.caption: Membership management replaces grant sprawl

blocks.text: A **service principal** is a machine identity. The **02:00 daily ETL** should not depend on `nikos@company.com`: if Nikos leaves, his account is **disabled** and production stops. Use `orders-etl-prod` instead.

blocks.title: Production ownership & writes → groups / service principals
blocks.text: Databricks recommends assigning **production ownership and write access** to **groups or service principals**, not personal users.

sections.title: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA & the Read Path
sections.hook: `USE` lets you through the doors but doesn't let you read anything. Reading a table takes three keys.

items.title: USE CATALOG means
points: they can **traverse / use** the catalog as a namespace
still subject to permissions on each object

blocks.text: Databricks states explicitly: `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` are **prerequisite access privileges** — on their own they do **not** grant `SELECT`.

blocks.code:
GRANT USE SCHEMA
ON SCHEMA ecommerce.gold
TO `analysts`;      -- still NOT "SELECT everything"

blocks.text:
USE CATALOG ecommerce      (door of the building)
        +
USE SCHEMA  gold           (door of the floor)
        +
SELECT      daily_sales    (key to the room)
        =
SELECT * FROM ecommerce.gold.daily_sales  ✓
blocks.caption: The read path: three keys
The minimum to read one table

blocks.label: Think first (source exercise §21): `analysts` have USE CATALOG ecommerce and USE SCHEMA ecommerce.gold, but no SELECT. What does `SELECT * FROM ecommerce.gold.daily_sales` do?
blocks.text: It **fails**. `USE` gives no permission on the **data** — it only lets you traverse the namespace.
**Debugging Case 2** — the mirror image: SELECT on `daily_revenue` ✅, USE CATALOG ✅, **USE SCHEMA ❌**. The query can still fail, because you **cannot traverse the schema**.

blocks.title: USE privileges are prerequisites, not data access
blocks.text: Reading needs **USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT** (on the table, or inherited). Missing any one → denied. Having only the USE pair → also denied.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when I have SELECT but still get PERMISSION_DENIED
questions: Do I (or my group) have USE CATALOG on the parent catalog?
Do I have USE SCHEMA on the exact parent schema — not on a sibling schema?
Is the SELECT on this object (or inherited from schema/catalog)?
Am I really the identity running the query?

sections.title: Inheritance, SELECT vs MODIFY, SHOW GRANTS & REVOKE
sections.hook: Grants flow down the hierarchy. That saves thousands of grants, and it explains why a REVOKE can leave access in place.

blocks.text: **Privilege inheritance**: a grant on a parent can flow to its children, following the Unity Catalog inheritance model.

blocks.code:
GRANT SELECT
ON SCHEMA ecommerce.gold
TO `analysts`;
-- flows to the tables/views inside ecommerce.gold

blocks.text:
CATALOG ecommerce        grant here → flows to all schemas below
└── SCHEMA gold          grant here → flows to all objects below
    ├── daily_sales       ← inherits
    ├── customer_360      ← inherits
    └── (new table)       ← inherits too
blocks.caption: Grants on parents flow to children

blocks.text: Databricks recommends using the hierarchy and inheritance to avoid **thousands of per-table grants**.

head: Privilege
Meaning
Typical principal
rows: narrower write capability instead of broad MODIFY
blocks.caption: SELECT vs MODIFY

blocks.text: **MODIFY** has historically covered **broad DML**. Current Unity Catalog also has **finer-grained DML privileges in beta** (e.g. `INSERT`), so you can grant narrower write rights than MODIFY. The basic model is still analyst → SELECT and engineer or pipeline SP → MODIFY, depending on the architecture.
**SHOW GRANTS** answers the most basic debugging question: **who has what?**

blocks.caption: Inspect every level of the hierarchy
REVOKE uses FROM, not TO

blocks.title: REVOKE on the table ≠ access gone
blocks.text: You can remove the **direct** table grant and the user still reads, because `SELECT` on the **schema** or **catalog** is inherited. Permission debugging must always inspect **inheritance**.

**Debugging Case 3**: a user had SELECT on `daily_revenue`. The admin runs REVOKE on the table, but the user **still reads**. Likely cause: `SELECT ON SCHEMA gold`, or a catalog-level inherited grant.

SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG prod_ecommerce        SELECT? ── yes → still readable
        │ no
SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA  prod_ecommerce.gold   SELECT? ── yes → still readable
        │ no
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE   ...daily_revenue      (revoked) → access really gone
blocks.caption: Case 3: inspect the whole hierarchy, not just the table

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a REVOKE didn't remove access
questions: Did I revoke from the right principal — the group the user actually belongs to?
Is there SELECT on the parent schema that the table inherits?
Is there SELECT (or ALL PRIVILEGES) on the parent catalog?
Is the user in another group that still holds a grant?
Is the user the owner (or does the user hold MANAGE) and so able to re-grant?

sections.title: Ownership, MANAGE, ALL PRIVILEGES & BROWSE
sections.hook: Some privileges let you change the rules rather than read data. Use them sparingly and give them to groups.

blocks.text: **Every securable has an owner.** The owner has far more power than plain SELECT. Typically the owner can:

blocks.code: ALTER TABLE prod.gold.revenue SET OWNER TO `data_platform_admins`;
blocks.caption: Transfer ownership to a group

blocks.text: **MANAGE** is a privilege for **delegated governance**: a principal with MANAGE can manage grants and ownership-related operations **without being the owner**.

blocks.code: GRANT MANAGE ON SCHEMA prod.gold TO `data_platform_admins`;

blocks.title: ALL PRIVILEGES is not literally everything
blocks.text: Current UC docs: **`MANAGE`, `EXTERNAL USE LOCATION` and `EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA` are NOT included in `ALL PRIVILEGES`.** Classic certification trap.

items.term: EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA / EXTERNAL USE LOCATION
items.def: Privileges that let **external (non-Databricks) engines** access UC data in a schema / location via UC's APIs. Must be granted explicitly — never via ALL PRIVILEGES.
Every applicable privilege on the securable **except** MANAGE / EXTERNAL USE … — and it is evaluated **dynamically**, so privileges added to the platform later are included automatically.

blocks.code:
-- common bad practice
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES
ON CATALOG prod_ecommerce
TO `all_company_users`;
blocks.caption: Don't do this

blocks.text: Why is that bad? It may allow **much more** than each principal needs, and `ALL PRIVILEGES` is **evaluated dynamically** — as new applicable privileges are added, they're included. Databricks recommends **restraint with both ALL PRIVILEGES and MANAGE**.

**BROWSE** allows **discoverability / metadata visibility** without data access. Users can discover that a dataset **exists**, then **request access** before running `SELECT`. Lineage visibility can also use BROWSE semantics for object discovery.

blocks.code: GRANT BROWSE ON CATALOG prod TO `account users`;
blocks.caption: Everyone can discover; nobody reads without SELECT

sections.title: Managed vs External Tables
sections.hook: The difference is who controls where the files live and when they die. It decides what DROP TABLE does to your data.

blocks.label: Think first: does "managed" mean the data sits inside Databricks' servers and "external" outside?
blocks.text: **No.** Both can live in **your own cloud object storage**. The difference is **who controls the location and lifecycle of the underlying files**.

Databricks: **managed assets** get UC governance **and** storage-lifecycle management; **external assets** get UC governance, but the storage lifecycle stays **your** (or an external system's) responsibility.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders (
  id     BIGINT,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2)
);                      -- no LOCATION → managed
blocks.caption: Managed table: Unity Catalog decides the path

blocks.text:
catalog / schema managed storage root
            │
            ▼
Unity-generated internal location
            │
            ▼
        Delta files
blocks.caption: Where a managed table's files go

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders_ext
USING DELTA
LOCATION 's3://company-data/orders/';   -- or the Azure/GCS equivalent
blocks.caption: External table: YOU specify the location

items.title: EXTERNAL TABLE — UC controls
points: — YOU control: storage location + storage lifecycle

head: Managed
External
rows: deleted by UC as part of the managed lifecycle
blocks.caption: The certification classic

blocks.title: DROP TABLE: managed vs external
blocks.text: `DROP TABLE managed_table` → UC handles metadata **and** underlying file lifecycle. `DROP TABLE external_table` → UC removes the metadata, but the **files remain**. Know this cold.
**Which is recommended?** For new Databricks-first workloads, Databricks generally recommends **managed tables** — more automation, optimization and governance integration.
**External tables make sense** when: existing data already lives at known paths; multiple non-Databricks systems control the storage lifecycle; migration constraints; interoperability requirements.
**External table lifecycle example.** `s3://company/legacy/orders/` already holds Delta data.

items: Prerequisite: the location falls under a **governed external location** + the principal has the required privileges.
UC now **registers metadata**. It does **not** necessarily rewrite the data.

blocks.title: Check the type before you DROP
blocks.text: `DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED <name>` shows **Type** (MANAGED / EXTERNAL) and **Location**. Ten seconds that prevent "where did my data go?" — or "why is my bucket still full?".

blocks.title: Ask yourself before / after a DROP TABLE
questions: Is this table MANAGED or EXTERNAL (DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED)?
If managed: am I OK with UC deleting the underlying files as part of the lifecycle?
If external: do I expect the files to stay — and who will clean them up?
Do other systems still read these files directly?

sections.title: Managed Storage, Storage Credentials & External Locations
sections.hook: This is where the bytes physically are, and how Databricks is allowed to reach them, one layer at a time.

blocks.text: Where does a managed table physically go? UC can have a **managed storage location** at three levels: **metastore, catalog, schema**. The **most specific (lowest) available** location wins.

schema managed location     ← highest priority (if set)
        │ else
catalog managed location
        │ else
metastore managed location
blocks.caption: Most specific managed location wins

blocks.text: Databricks now often recommends **catalog-level managed storage** as the isolation boundary.

blocks.caption: Managed locations on catalog and schema

blocks.title: Requirements for MANAGED LOCATION
blocks.text: The path must lie **under a Unity Catalog external location**, and you need the **`CREATE MANAGED STORAGE`** privilege (on that external location).

**Storage credential.** Databricks must authenticate to the cloud for `s3://company-raw-data/`. You don't want every user holding an **AWS access key + secret key**. So UC has an object that **abstracts a long-term cloud credential**:

A storage credential alone answers "**with which identity** can I talk to the cloud?" — not "**which path** do we govern?". The **external location** combines **cloud path + storage credential** and is itself a securable.

AWS IAM role / Azure identity
        │
        ▼
Storage Credential      "IAM role X"
        │
        ▼
External Location       path = s3://company/raw/
        │               credential = IAM role X
        ▼
External Table / External Volume
        │
        ▼
      Files
blocks.caption: The full chain — one of the most important UC diagrams
External location = path + credential; grant on the location

blocks.text: **Why not grant on the storage credential directly?** A credential may reach a **huge storage scope**. An external location like `s3://company/finance/` scopes access to **that path only**. Databricks recommends granting e.g. `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` on the **external location** rather than on the credential.

credential A
├── s3://company/raw/       (external location 1)
├── s3://company/archive/   (external location 2)
└── s3://company/shared/    (external location 3)
     each with its own UC access boundary
blocks.caption: One credential, many external locations

items.title: Storage credential
points: HOW Databricks authenticates to cloud storage
wraps IAM role / managed identity / service account

items.title: External table
points: table METADATA pointing at tabular data
not a synonym of external location

blocks.title: Two confusable pairs
blocks.text: **Storage credential vs external location**: identity vs path + identity. **External location vs external table**: governed storage path vs table metadata pointing at data inside that path. Not synonyms.

**Debugging Case 4**: the **managed** table works, the **external** table fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED` / a storage access error. External storage adds **extra layers**: external location, storage credential, workspace binding, cloud IAM.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a managed table works but the external one fails
questions: Is the table's LOCATION covered by an external location at all?
Do I (or the job's principal) hold the needed privilege on that external location?
Is the external location / storage credential bound to this workspace?
Does the cloud IAM role behind the storage credential actually allow this path?
Was the IAM role / trust policy changed or the bucket policy tightened recently?

sections.title: Volumes: Governed Files
sections.hook: Not everything is a table. PDFs, images, configs and raw files get UC governance through volumes.

blocks.text: A **table** is for tabular data: rows / columns with SQL / DataFrame semantics. What about **PDF, JPEG, JSON config, ML files, checkpoints, text documents, binary artifacts, raw files**? You don't want to make them all tables.
**Volume** = a Unity Catalog **governed storage object for non-tabular / file-based data**.

blocks.title: Volume = governed file-path semantics
blocks.text: Databricks recommends **table names** for tables and **`/Volumes/...`** paths for direct non-tabular file access, instead of writing raw cloud URIs everywhere.

head: Need
Table
Volume
blocks.caption: Tables vs volumes — an easy certification question

blocks.text: **Debugging Case 5**: the user has USE CATALOG ✅ and USE SCHEMA ✅, but `open("/Volumes/.../file.json")` fails. Check **READ VOLUME** — and for writes, **WRITE VOLUME** too.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a /Volumes/ file can't be read or written
questions: Is the path really /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/… (right names, right order)?
Do I have USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents?
Do I have READ VOLUME on this volume (not SELECT — that's for tables)?
For writes: do I also have WRITE VOLUME?
If it's an external volume: are the external location / credential / cloud IAM fine?

blocks.title: SELECT does nothing for volumes
blocks.text: Granting `SELECT` on a schema doesn't open its volumes. Volumes use **READ VOLUME / WRITE VOLUME**.

sections.title: Workspace Bindings & the UC Compute Requirement
sections.hook: Correct grants are not the whole story. The workspace you are in and the compute you use can still block access.

blocks.text: You have two workspaces, `dev-workspace` and `prod-workspace`, and a catalog `prod`. You can say: **the `prod` catalog may be used only from specific workspaces.** That is a **workspace binding**.

catalog prod  (bound to prod-workspace only)
                       ▲        ✗
                       │        │
prod-workspace ────────┘        └──────── dev-workspace
   access possible                  access FAILS
                                    (even with all grants)
blocks.caption: Workspace binding: a separate access-control mechanism

blocks.text: UC uses workspace bindings as a **separate access-control mechanism** for **catalogs, external locations and storage credentials**. So the user can hold the permission and access still fails, because the **current workspace has no binding** to the catalog.
**Debugging implication.** The user has USE CATALOG `prod`, USE SCHEMA `prod.finance`, SELECT `prod.finance.payroll` — and still fails. Possible cause: **`prod` catalog not bound to this workspace.**

blocks.title: User privilege ≠ the only authorization boundary
blocks.text: Grants answer "may this principal do X?". Workspace bindings answer "may X be used **from this workspace** at all?". Both must say yes.

**UC compute requirement.** Having permissions isn't enough: the **compute must be Unity Catalog-compatible**. Classic compute with **Standard** or **Dedicated** access mode can access UC; **serverless** and **Databricks SQL** compute support it.

permissions correct
        +
wrong / legacy compute (not UC-compatible)
        =
still failure
blocks.caption: Correct grants on the wrong compute still fail

blocks.title: Recap → Chapters 7 & 8
blocks.text: Access modes Standard vs Dedicated (Chapter 7) and SQL-warehouse Gate 2 (Chapter 8) meet here: the access mode is what makes classic compute **UC-capable**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when every grant looks right but access still fails
questions: Which workspace am I in — and is the catalog (or external location / credential) bound to it?
Would the same query work from the prod workspace?
Is my compute UC-compatible: Standard/Dedicated access mode, serverless, or a SQL warehouse?
Am I on an old/legacy cluster configuration someone left running?

sections.title: Row Filters, Column Masks & ABAC
sections.hook: SELECT decides whether you can query a table. Fine-grained policies decide which rows and which values you see.

blocks.text: **Row-level security.** Table `sales(country, revenue)` has GR, DE, FR rows. You want: Greek team → only GR rows; German team → only DE rows.
A **row filter** is a **SQL UDF applied at query time**: rows where it returns **false** are removed.

SELECT * FROM sales
        │
        ▼
   row filter UDF
        ├── TRUE  → row visible
        └── FALSE → row removed
blocks.caption: Row filter at query time

blocks.code:
CREATE FUNCTION security.country_filter(country STRING)
RETURN
  CASE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('global_sales') THEN TRUE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('greece_sales') AND country = 'GR' THEN TRUE
    ELSE FALSE
  END;

ALTER TABLE ecommerce.gold.sales
SET ROW FILTER security.country_filter
ON (country);
blocks.caption: Row filter: UDF + ALTER TABLE … SET ROW FILTER … ON (col)

blocks.title: Design production UDFs carefully
blocks.text: The pattern above is the basic mechanism; production filter functions need careful design (every group covered, default FALSE, tested).
**Column mask.** Table `customer_id, name, email, salary`: analysts need the rows but not the real salary. A mask is a **query-time policy on a column value**.

stored value:            5000
query as finance_admin:  5000
query as analyst:        ****   (or NULL / bucketed)
blocks.caption: Same stored value, different visible value

blocks.code:
CREATE FUNCTION security.mask_salary(salary DECIMAL(10,2))
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('finance_admins') THEN salary
  ELSE NULL
END;

ALTER TABLE ecommerce.gold.employees
ALTER COLUMN salary SET MASK security.mask_salary;
blocks.caption: Column mask: UDF + ALTER COLUMN … SET MASK

blocks.text: **ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control).** For 5 tables you can attach filters/masks one by one. For **10,000 tables** that doesn't scale. ABAC uses **governed tags** (e.g. `sensitivity = pii`) plus **policies** (e.g. if a column is tagged pii → mask it for users without privilege).

blocks.caption: Tag once; the policy follows the tag

blocks.text: Databricks now recommends ABAC for **centralized, tag-driven policies** across many objects. ABAC can apply **row filters, column masks**, and now **policy-based GRANT/DENY** capabilities in supported scopes.

items.title: ABAC
points: new tagged table tomorrow → automatically covered

blocks.text: **Debugging Case 6**: "I have SELECT, why do I see `****`?" Because **SELECT ≠ unfiltered raw visibility**. Fine-grained policies change row/column visibility. Check **column mask, row filter, ABAC**.

blocks.title: SELECT ≠ seeing everything
blocks.text: Missing rows or masked values with a successful query is not a permission bug in the grants. It is a **row filter / column mask / ABAC** policy doing its job.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a query succeeds but rows are missing or values are masked
questions: Does this table have a row filter (which function, on which column)?
Does this column have a mask?
Is an ABAC policy matching a tag on this table/column?
Which groups am I in — does the policy function check a group I'm not in (is_account_group_member)?
Is the masking intended for my role, or is my group membership wrong?

debug.symptom: `PERMISSION_DENIED` (or INSUFFICIENT_PRIVILEGES) on a Unity Catalog object, e.g. `SELECT * FROM prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue`.
askYourself: Which principal is ACTUALLY executing — me, a job run-as, a pipeline service principal?

steps.why: Every grant is evaluated for the executing principal.
steps.code:
SELECT current_user();  -- interactive
-- jobs/pipelines: check the run-as identity in settings

steps.do: Check the workspace binding of the catalog / external location.
steps.why: A binding can block access despite perfect grants.

steps.do: Show grants top-down for that principal.
steps.why: USE CATALOG → USE SCHEMA → object privilege; inheritance included.

steps.do: If the query succeeds but rows/values look wrong, inspect filters, masks and ABAC.
steps.why: SELECT ≠ unfiltered raw visibility.

steps.do: For external tables/volumes, follow the storage chain.
steps.why: External location → storage credential → cloud IAM.

steps.do: Confirm the compute is UC-compatible.
steps.why: Correct permissions + wrong legacy compute = still failure.

Workspace not bound to the catalog
debug.fix: Fix the exact missing layer for the exact principal (usually a group or service principal) — never "give me admin".
debug.mnemonic: I Bet Cats Sit On Fluffy Silk Cushions — Identity · Binding · Catalog · Schema · Object · Fine-grained · Storage · Compute

debug.title: Case 1 — notebook works, job fails (wrong identity)
debug.symptom: Your notebook reads the table; the scheduled job running the same code fails with PERMISSION_DENIED.
askYourself: Is the job running as a different identity than me?
Which service principal is the run-as identity?
Does that service principal have USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and the object privilege?
Was the run-as recently changed?
Am I tempted to make it run as my personal user — and why is that wrong for production?

steps.do: Open the job settings and read the run-as identity.
steps.why: The identity that presses Run is not necessarily the workload identity.

steps.do: Show grants for that service principal down the hierarchy.
steps.why: Find the exact missing privilege.

steps.do: Grant only what the job needs to the service principal.
steps.why: Least privilege for machine identities.
steps.code: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.silver.orders TO `orders-etl-sp`;

rootCauses: Job runs as `orders-etl-sp`, which lacks SELECT
Run-as changed to an under-privileged identity
debug.fix: Grant the missing privilege(s) to the job's service principal; keep production on service principals, not personal users.

debug.title: Case 2 — SELECT exists but USE SCHEMA doesn't
debug.symptom: User has SELECT on `prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue` (and USE CATALOG) but the query is denied.
askYourself: Do I have USE CATALOG on the parent catalog?
Do I have USE SCHEMA on this exact schema — not on a sibling like silver?
Is the SELECT on this object or inherited?
Am I the identity that holds these grants?

steps.do: Show grants on the schema.
steps.why: USE SCHEMA is a prerequisite for data access.

steps.do: Grant USE SCHEMA to the group.
steps.why: Adds only the missing prerequisite.
steps.code: GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold TO `analysts`;

rootCauses: USE SCHEMA granted on the wrong schema
debug.fix: Grant USE SCHEMA (and USE CATALOG if missing) — SELECT alone can't traverse the namespace.

debug.title: Case 3 — REVOKE done, access remains
debug.symptom: Admin ran `REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue FROM analysts`, yet analysts still read the table.
askYourself: Did I revoke from the group the user actually reads through?
Is there SELECT on the parent schema that the table inherits?
Is there SELECT or ALL PRIVILEGES on the parent catalog?
Is the user in another group with a grant?
Is the user owner or MANAGE holder (able to re-grant)?

steps.do: Show grants at schema and catalog level.
steps.why: Inherited grants survive a table-level revoke.
steps.code:
SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold;
SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG prod_ecommerce;

steps.do: Restructure: move SELECT from schema to the specific tables (or move the sensitive table to another schema).
steps.why: You can't block an inherited grant by revoking lower down.

debug.fix: Find the inherited grant and restructure where SELECT is granted; always inspect the hierarchy.

debug.title: Case 4 — managed table works, external table fails
debug.symptom: Managed tables work; an external table returns PERMISSION_DENIED or a storage access error.
askYourself: Do the UC grants work (does a managed table in the same schema work)?
What is the table's LOCATION?
Is that path under an external location — and do I have privileges on it?
Is the external location / storage credential bound to this workspace?
Does the cloud IAM identity behind the storage credential allow this path?

steps.do: Get the location.
steps.why: Know which path you're dealing with.

steps.do: Check external locations covering it.
steps.why: No governed path → no access.

steps.do: Check bindings and the storage credential.
steps.why: Bindings also apply to external locations and credentials.

steps.do: Escalate to the cloud team for IAM.
steps.why: UC can't grant more than the cloud identity is allowed.

rootCauses: No external location for the path
Missing privilege on the external location
debug.fix: Repair the failing storage layer (external location, credential, binding or cloud IAM) — never hand out raw cloud keys.
debug.mnemonic: External = extra layers: Location · Credential · Binding · IAM

debug.title: Case 5 — /Volumes file inaccessible
debug.symptom: `open("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/documents/file.json")` fails although the user has USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA.
askYourself: Is the path /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/… in the right order?
Do I have READ VOLUME on this volume?
For writes, do I also have WRITE VOLUME?
Am I using SELECT/MODIFY by mistake (table privileges)?
If it's an external volume, is the storage chain OK?

steps.do: Verify the path.
steps.why: Swapped names point to a non-existent volume.

steps.do: Grant READ VOLUME (and WRITE VOLUME for writes).
steps.why: Volume privileges are separate from table privileges.
steps.code: GRANT READ VOLUME, WRITE VOLUME ON VOLUME ecommerce.raw.documents TO `data_engineers`;

debug.fix: Grant READ VOLUME (plus WRITE VOLUME for writes) on the volume.

debug.title: Case 6 — "I have SELECT, why do I see ****?"
debug.symptom: Query succeeds, but salary shows `****` / NULL, or rows are missing.
askYourself: Did the query succeed (so grants are fine)?
Is there a column mask on this column?
Is there a row filter on this table?
Does an ABAC policy match a tag on this table/column?
Which groups am I in — does the policy check a group I'm not in?

steps.do: Inspect the table definition for filters/masks.
steps.why: Masks and filters are attached to the table/column.

steps.do: Check ABAC policies and tags in Catalog Explorer.
steps.why: Tag-driven policies apply without per-table attachment.

steps.do: Decide: intended? If access is approved, change group membership — don't drop the policy.
steps.why: The policy is doing its job.

rootCauses: User not in the privileged group
debug.fix: Explain that SELECT ≠ unfiltered visibility; adjust group membership only if the business approves.
debug.mnemonic: SELECT opens the door, policies dim the lights

debug.title: Grants correct, still denied — workspace binding
debug.symptom: User has USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT, but the query fails in one workspace and works in another.
askYourself: Which workspace am I in?
Is the catalog bound only to specific workspaces?
Are the external location / storage credential bound to this workspace?
Should this workspace have access at all (isolation by design)?

steps.do: Compare the same query from another workspace.
steps.why: Same principal + same grants + different result → binding.

steps.do: Check the catalog's workspace bindings in Catalog Explorer.
steps.why: Bindings are a separate access-control mechanism.

steps.do: Use the bound workspace, or request a binding change if intended.
steps.why: Grants can't override a missing binding.

rootCauses: Catalog not bound to this workspace
debug.fix: Run from a bound workspace or have an admin add the binding — if the isolation design allows it.

debug.title: Grants correct, still denied — compute not UC-compatible
debug.symptom: Same user and grants work on a SQL warehouse but fail on an old cluster.
askYourself: Does the same query work on a SQL warehouse or serverless?
What is this cluster's access mode?
Is it Standard or Dedicated — or a legacy configuration?
Did someone reuse an old cluster definition?

steps.do: Compare on serverless / SQL warehouse.
steps.why: Isolates the compute layer.

steps.do: Check the access mode in the cluster config.
steps.why: Standard/Dedicated are UC-capable.

steps.do: Switch to UC-compatible compute.
steps.why: Permissions correct + wrong legacy compute = still failure.

askYourself: Was the table MANAGED or EXTERNAL?

If external: did I expect the files to stay?

askYourself: What is the dashboard's upstream table (lineage)?
Is the value already wrong in gold.daily_revenue?
Is it wrong in silver.orders?
Is it wrong in bronze.orders?

steps.why: Lineage gives the path upstream.

pitfalls.title: Thinking Unity Catalog stores your data
pitfalls.text: UC holds metadata, permissions, lineage and storage references; the bytes are in S3/ADLS/GCS.
pitfalls.fix: Separate governance (UC) from storage (cloud) in every explanation and debug.

pitfalls.title: Putting the workspace in the namespace
pitfalls.text: A notebook lives in a workspace; tables are registered in the metastore. `catalog.schema.object` has no workspace level.
pitfalls.fix: Remember: workspace = operational environment; metastore = regional governance container.

pitfalls.title: One metastore per project
pitfalls.text: Metastores are regional (usually one per region). Isolation starts at the catalog level.
pitfalls.fix: Create a new catalog, not a new metastore.

pitfalls.title: CREATE SCHEMA with only CREATE SCHEMA
pitfalls.text: Schema creation also needs USE CATALOG on the parent catalog.
pitfalls.fix: Grant USE CATALOG + CREATE SCHEMA on the parent catalog.

pitfalls.title: USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA mistaken for data access
pitfalls.text: USE privileges are traversal prerequisites; they never grant SELECT.
pitfalls.fix: Read path = USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT.

pitfalls.title: SELECT without USE SCHEMA
pitfalls.text: SELECT on a table is useless if the parent schema can't be traversed.
pitfalls.fix: Grant USE SCHEMA on the exact parent schema.

pitfalls.title: REVOKE on a table assumed to remove access
pitfalls.text: Inherited SELECT on the schema or catalog keeps access alive.
pitfalls.fix: SHOW GRANTS on schema and catalog; restructure grants.

pitfalls.title: REVOKE … TO
pitfalls.text: REVOKE uses FROM, GRANT uses TO.
pitfalls.fix: REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE t FROM `group`;

pitfalls.title: ALL PRIVILEGES assumed to be everything
pitfalls.text: MANAGE, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION and EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA are excluded.
pitfalls.fix: Grant MANAGE explicitly where delegated governance is intended.

pitfalls.title: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES to all users
pitfalls.text: Violates least privilege, and ALL PRIVILEGES grows dynamically as new privileges appear.
pitfalls.fix: Grant minimal, specific privileges to groups; be restrained with ALL PRIVILEGES and MANAGE.

pitfalls.title: Personal owners and personal run-as in production
pitfalls.text: When the person leaves, ownership/jobs break.
pitfalls.fix: Groups own production objects; service principals run pipelines.

pitfalls.title: BROWSE confused with SELECT
pitfalls.text: BROWSE only reveals that objects exist (metadata).
pitfalls.fix: Use BROWSE for discovery; grant SELECT only after an access request.

pitfalls.title: Managed = inside Databricks servers
pitfalls.text: Both managed and external data can live in your cloud storage; the difference is who controls location and lifecycle.
pitfalls.fix: Ask "who controls the files' location and lifecycle?"

pitfalls.title: Dropping an external table to free storage
pitfalls.text: DROP on an external table removes metadata only; files remain.
pitfalls.fix: Delete files with storage tooling if truly unwanted; check type before DROP.

pitfalls.title: Dropping a managed table you still need
pitfalls.text: For managed tables UC handles deletion of the underlying files.
pitfalls.fix: DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED before DROP; know the type.

pitfalls.title: MANAGED LOCATION on an ungoverned path
pitfalls.text: Managed locations must be under a UC external location and need CREATE MANAGED STORAGE.
pitfalls.fix: Create/choose an external location first; grant CREATE MANAGED STORAGE.

pitfalls.title: Granting on the storage credential instead of the external location
pitfalls.text: Credentials can reach a huge storage scope.
pitfalls.fix: Grant CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE etc. on the external location (path-scoped).

pitfalls.title: External location vs external table confusion
pitfalls.text: Location = governed path; table = metadata pointing at data in that path.
pitfalls.fix: Keep the chain: credential → location → table/volume → files.

pitfalls.title: Using SELECT for volumes
pitfalls.text: Volumes use READ VOLUME / WRITE VOLUME.
pitfalls.fix: Grant USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + READ VOLUME (+ WRITE VOLUME).

pitfalls.title: Ignoring workspace bindings
pitfalls.text: A catalog/location/credential may be bound to specific workspaces; grants can't override that.
pitfalls.fix: Check bindings when grants look right but access fails in one workspace.

pitfalls.title: Correct grants on non-UC compute
pitfalls.text: Legacy compute fails even with perfect permissions.
pitfalls.fix: Use Standard/Dedicated, serverless or SQL warehouses.

pitfalls.title: SELECT expected to show raw values
pitfalls.text: Row filters, column masks and ABAC change visibility at query time.
pitfalls.fix: Check filters/masks/ABAC and group membership.

pitfalls.title: Row filter defaulting to TRUE
pitfalls.text: ELSE TRUE shows every row to unmatched users.
pitfalls.fix: Deny by default: ELSE FALSE.

flashcards.q: The four questions of the Phase-3 mental model?
flashcards.a: WHO? → WHAT OBJECT? → WHAT ACTION? → WHERE ARE THE BYTES?
Permissions scattered across storage, notebooks, clusters and BI tools — no single answer to "who has what?".
Metadata + namespace + permissions + ownership + lineage + governance policies + storage references — not the bytes.
The metastore.

flashcards.q: How many metastores per region, typically?
flashcards.a: One; many workspaces in the region attach to it.
Workspace = operational development environment. Metastore = regional UC governance container.

flashcards.q: Three conditions for two workspaces to see the same object?
flashcards.a: Same metastore + principal has permission + no workspace binding forbids it.
Metastore = top regional governance container. Catalog = primary logical/data isolation container inside it.
The catalog.
Tables, views, volumes, models, functions (and materialized views, streaming tables …).
USE CATALOG + CREATE SCHEMA on the parent catalog.
CREATE CATALOG on the metastore.
A UC object on which privileges can be granted to principals (catalog, schema, table, volume, external location, storage credential, function …).
User, group, service principal.
At the account level; prefer groups over individual users.
Stable machine identity decoupled from employee lifecycle.
No — USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA are prerequisites only.

flashcards.q: Minimum grants to read one table?
flashcards.a: USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT (on table or inherited).
SELECT exists but USE SCHEMA is missing → can't traverse the schema.

flashcards.q: What does GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA do to new tables?
flashcards.a: They inherit it — inheritance covers current and future child objects.
SELECT reads; MODIFY writes/changes data (broad DML). Finer DML like INSERT exists in beta.
SHOW GRANTS ON <TABLE|SCHEMA|CATALOG> <name>;
REVOKE <privilege> ON <type> <name> FROM <principal>;

flashcards.q: Case 3: REVOKE on table but user still reads — why?
flashcards.a: Inherited SELECT on the schema or catalog.
Manage privileges, modify/manage the object, transfer ownership.
Groups (e.g. data_platform_admins), not individuals.
Delegated governance: manage grants/ownership-related operations without being owner.

flashcards.q: What is excluded from ALL PRIVILEGES?
flashcards.a: MANAGE, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION, EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA.

flashcards.q: Why is ALL PRIVILEGES risky over time?
flashcards.a: It's evaluated dynamically — new applicable privileges are added automatically.
Discovering that objects exist (metadata) without data access.

flashcards.q: Managed vs external — the real difference?
flashcards.a: Who controls the files' location and lifecycle (UC vs you/external system).
UC handles metadata and deletion of underlying files.
Metadata removed; files remain.

flashcards.q: When does an external table make sense?
flashcards.a: Existing data at known paths, non-Databricks lifecycle control, migration constraints, interoperability.
Schema > catalog > metastore (most specific wins).
Path under a UC external location + CREATE MANAGED STORAGE.
UC object abstracting a long-term cloud identity (IAM role / managed identity / service account).
Cloud path + storage credential, as a securable.
Cloud IAM → storage credential → external location → external table/volume → files.

flashcards.q: Why grant on external location, not credential?
flashcards.a: Path-scoped least privilege.
External location, storage credential, workspace binding, cloud IAM.
A UC-governed object for non-tabular/file data, accessed via /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/…
READ VOLUME, WRITE VOLUME (+ USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA).
Metadata removed; files remain.
A restriction on which workspaces can use a catalog, external location or storage credential.
Classic Standard/Dedicated, serverless, Databricks SQL.
SQL UDF applied at query time; rows where it returns false are removed.

flashcards.a: ALTER TABLE t SET ROW FILTER f ON (col);

Attribute-based access control: governed tags + central policies (filters, masks, GRANT/DENY) across many objects.
SELECT ≠ unfiltered raw visibility — column mask / row filter / ABAC.
Automatic, down to column level, across workspaces sharing the metastore.
