flashcards.q: Why can a job fail while your notebook works?
flashcards.a: It may run as a service principal with different privileges.

exercises.q: Put the four Unity Catalog questions in the order the mental model asks them.
items: WHAT ACTION? (USE / SELECT / MODIFY / CREATE / READ VOLUME)
WHERE ARE THE BYTES? (managed storage or external location)
exercises.explain: The model goes from the **identity**, to the **object** in the hierarchy, to the **action** (privilege), and finally to the **physical bytes** in cloud storage. Most permission bugs sit in one of these four layers.

exercises.q: Sort each item into the question of the mental model it answers.
exercises.explain: Principals answer **WHO**; securables in the hierarchy answer **WHAT OBJECT**; privileges answer **WHAT ACTION**; managed storage / external locations answer **WHERE ARE THE BYTES**. Mixing these layers up is the root of most UC confusion.

exercises.q: Permissions for the same data live in S3 bucket policies, Azure Storage ACLs, notebook ACLs, cluster settings and the BI tool. What is this called?
why: Correct — many systems, many permission models.
Least privilege is about giving minimal rights, not where rights live.
Data isolation is a design goal (often a catalog boundary).
Workspace binding is a UC feature restricting which workspaces see an object.
exercises.explain: When permissions are scattered across storage, notebooks, clusters and BI tools you have **fragmented governance** — no single place answers "who has what?". UC exists to make governance **central**. Least privilege is a principle, not this problem.

exercises.q: Which governance question can bucket-level storage permissions alone **never** answer?
exercises.explain: Storage permissions know about **paths and identities**, not about **tables, columns, pipelines or dashboards**. Questions like "which dashboard uses this column?" need **lineage**, which UC captures centrally.

exercises.q: Unity Catalog stores the Parquet bytes of your Delta tables inside its own database.
exercises.explain: False. UC holds **metadata, namespace, permissions, ownership, lineage, policies and storage references**. The actual data files live in **cloud object storage** (S3 / ADLS / GCS) — even for managed tables.

exercises.q: Which items does Unity Catalog hold? (choose all)
exercises.explain: UC = metadata + namespace + permissions + ownership + lineage + governance policies + storage references. The **data files** stay in cloud storage; UC only points to (or manages) them.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: S3, ADLS and GCS are **cloud object stores** where the bytes live. Unity Catalog is the **governance layer** that points at them — it is not storage.

exercises.q: Explain to a new colleague, in 3–4 sentences, why a company with 100 developers and data in S3 folders needs Unity Catalog.
exercises.model: Without central governance, permissions live in many places (bucket policies, notebooks, clusters, BI tools), so nobody can answer who may read payroll, who owns a table, which pipeline created it or which dashboard uses a column. Unity Catalog adds one hierarchical governance layer over the storage: every asset is a securable object in a catalog.schema.object namespace, privileges go to users, groups and service principals, and lineage is captured automatically. The bytes stay in cloud storage — UC governs metadata, permissions and storage references.
rubric: UC = one central, hierarchical governance layer
UC does not store the bytes
exercises.explain: A strong answer names the problem (fragmented governance), the solution (central hierarchical layer with securables, privileges, principals) and the boundary (UC governs; storage keeps the bytes).

exercises.q: Order these levels from top (broadest) to bottom.
exercises.explain: Metastore is the top-level container, then catalog (first name), schema (second name), object (third name). The workspace is **not** part of this chain.

exercises.q: Databricks calls one level "the primary unit of data isolation". Which?
why: Correct.
Schema is finer-grained organization inside a catalog.
Usually one per region, shared by many workspaces — too broad.
Not part of the namespace.
exercises.explain: The **catalog** is the primary data-isolation unit (e.g. `dev` vs `prod`). The schema is a finer organizational/access layer; the metastore is regional and usually shared; the workspace is an operational environment, not a namespace level.

exercises.q: A metastore is NOT three of these. Which option is the odd one out because it IS what a metastore is?
options: the top-level container for UC metadata and permissions
exercises.explain: A metastore is the **top-level container for Unity Catalog metadata and permissions**. It is not a table, not a schema, not a storage bucket and not a workspace.

exercises.q: Which of these does the metastore hold metadata about? (choose all)
exercises.explain: The metastore tracks catalogs, tables, volumes, external locations, credentials, shares and permissions. **Clusters** are compute resources in a workspace, not metastore objects.

exercises.q: A company has 3 workspaces in Europe and 2 workspaces in the US, using the typical pattern. How many Unity Catalog metastores do they usually have?
exercises.explain: Typically **one metastore per region**, shared by all workspaces in that region: one for Europe, one for the US = **2**. You don't create one metastore per workspace or per project.

exercises.q: Where does each thing belong?
exercises.explain: Notebooks, jobs and compute are **workspace** objects (where you work). Catalogs, tables, external locations and credentials are **metastore** objects (where data is governed) — which is why several workspaces can see the same table.

exercises.q: Workspace B wants to query `prod.sales.orders`, created from workspace A. Which conditions must hold? (choose all)
options: Both workspaces are attached to the same metastore
The principal has the needed privileges
No workspace binding blocks the catalog in workspace B
The table was re-created inside workspace B
exercises.explain: The table is registered in the **metastore**, not in workspace A. B sees it if it shares the metastore, the principal is granted access, and no **workspace binding** excludes B. Nothing needs to be re-created.

exercises.q: A team lead wants to isolate a new project's data. What is the default Databricks recommendation?
options: Create a new catalog (and grants) inside the existing regional metastore
Create a new metastore for the project
Create a new workspace — that isolates the data
Create a new S3 bucket and skip UC
why: Correct.
Metastores are regional containers; not one per project.
A workspace is an operational environment; data stays in the shared metastore.
Skipping UC brings back fragmented governance.
exercises.explain: Isolation usually starts at the **catalog** level. A new metastore per project is **not** the default pattern (usually one per region), and a new workspace does not isolate governed data on its own — workspaces sharing a metastore see the same objects.

exercises.q: Match each part of `prod.finance.payroll` to its level.
exercises.explain: The three-level namespace is **catalog.schema.object**. The first name is the isolation boundary, the second organizes, the third is the actual asset.

exercises.q: Which one cannot be the third name (the object) in `catalog.schema.object`?
exercises.explain: Objects inside a schema include tables, views, volumes, functions, models, materialized views and streaming tables. A **workspace** is an operational environment outside the namespace.

exercises.q: A company is designing catalogs. Classify each design.
exercises.explain: All three are valid; there is no single right structure. Databricks' rule: catalogs should be **meaningful isolation boundaries** (environment, business unit, team, project) so grants stay simple.

exercises.q: Databricks prescribes exactly one correct catalog layout: one catalog per environment (dev/test/prod).
exercises.explain: False. Environment, business unit, team, project or mixed layouts are all valid. The guidance is that catalogs represent **meaningful isolation boundaries** so hierarchical grants stay simple.

exercises.q: You run `USE CATALOG prod; USE SCHEMA sales;` and then `SELECT * FROM orders;`. Which table do you read, and why is this risky in production code?
options: `prod.sales.orders`; the short name depends on session context, so the same code may read another table elsewhere
`orders` in the default `hive_metastore`; USE is ignored by SELECT
An error — short names are not allowed in Unity Catalog
`prod.sales.orders`; there is no risk because USE is permanent for the workspace
exercises.explain: Unqualified names resolve against the **current catalog and schema**. That works, but the same code run with a different context resolves to a different object — so production code prefers **fully qualified names**. USE only affects the current session.

exercises.q: Complete the statements to create the catalog and an idempotent schema.
exercises.explain: `CREATE CATALOG` makes the catalog, `USE CATALOG` sets the session context, and `IF NOT EXISTS` makes the schema creation safe to re-run.

exercises.q: Maria runs `CREATE SCHEMA ecommerce.gold;` and gets a permission error. Which pair of privileges does she typically need?
why: Correct — hierarchical.
CREATE SCHEMA is granted on the parent catalog.
SELECT reads data; it doesn't create schemas.
That creates catalogs, not schemas.
exercises.explain: Schema creation needs `USE CATALOG` **and** `CREATE SCHEMA` on the **parent catalog**. `CREATE CATALOG` is for making catalogs; `SELECT` is a data-reading privilege.

exercises.q: To create a new catalog you typically need the `CREATE CATALOG` privilege on the metastore.
exercises.explain: True. Catalogs are children of the metastore, so `CREATE CATALOG` is granted on the metastore — the same hierarchical logic as `CREATE SCHEMA` on the parent catalog.

exercises.q: Write SQL that creates catalog `ecommerce` (only if missing), creates schema `silver` in it (only if missing), and then sets both as the current context.
keywords: create schema if not exists ecommerce.silver
exercises.explain: `IF NOT EXISTS` makes setup scripts re-runnable; `USE CATALOG` / `USE SCHEMA` only set the session context — they don't grant anything.

exercises.q: `CREATE SCHEMA ecommerce.gold;` fails with a permission error for Maria. Walk it like an engineer.

steps.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: Who is actually running the statement (Maria interactively, or a job's service principal)?
options.fb: Right — always confirm the identity before reading grants.

options.text: Ask an admin for ALL PRIVILEGES on the metastore.
options.fb: That breaks least privilege and teaches you nothing about the cause.

options.text: Re-create the catalog.
options.fb: Destructive and unrelated — the catalog exists.

steps.prompt: Maria runs it herself. Which grants do you inspect?

options.text: `SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG ecommerce;` — look for USE CATALOG and CREATE SCHEMA for Maria or her groups.
options.fb: Correct: schema creation is authorized on the parent catalog.

options.text: `SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE ecommerce.gold.x;`
options.fb: The schema doesn't exist yet; table grants are irrelevant.

options.text: Check the cluster's autoscaling settings.
options.fb: Compute sizing has nothing to do with a privilege error.

steps.prompt: She has CREATE SCHEMA but no USE CATALOG. Fix?

options.text: `GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG ecommerce TO` her group.
options.fb: Yes — CREATE SCHEMA needs USE CATALOG as a prerequisite.

options.text: Grant SELECT on the catalog.
options.fb: SELECT reads data; it doesn't let you traverse/use the catalog for creation.

options.text: Grant CREATE CATALOG on the metastore.
options.fb: Over-privileged and still not the missing piece.

exercises.q: Classify each item.
exercises.explain: Principals receive grants, securables are what grants are **on**, privileges are the **action** granted. External locations and storage credentials are securables too — you grant privileges on them.

exercises.q: A storage credential is a securable object in Unity Catalog.
exercises.explain: True. Any object registered in UC on which grants can be given is securable — including **storage credentials** and **external locations**, not only tables.

exercises.q: 4 analysts each need SELECT on 50 gold tables. How many GRANT statements do you need if you grant per individual user (one table per statement)?
exercises.explain: 4 users × 50 tables = **200** grants. With a group `analysts` you grant 50 (or 1 at schema level with inheritance), and a new hire needs **0** new grants — just group membership.

exercises.q: When Maria joins the analytics team and all grants were made to group `analysts`, you must add her to each of the 200 table grants.
exercises.explain: False. You add Maria to the `analysts` group; **zero** grants change. That's exactly why groups are preferred: membership management instead of permission sprawl.

exercises.q: Databricks recommends provisioning users, groups and service principals at the workspace level, separately in each workspace.
exercises.explain: False. The recommendation is to provision principals at the **account level** (and use groups), so the same identities work across workspaces attached to the metastore.

exercises.q: A production job definition. Which line is the governance problem?
exercises.explain: A production job should not run as a **personal user**: if Nikos leaves and his account is disabled, the 02:00 ETL stops. Run it as a **service principal** — a stable machine identity decoupled from employee lifecycle.

exercises.q: Complete the grant that lets group `analysts` read the table.
exercises.explain: Grammar: **GRANT** privilege **ON** object-type object **TO** principal. `FROM` belongs to REVOKE.

exercises.q: (Source exercise §21) `analysts` have `USE CATALOG ecommerce` and `USE SCHEMA ecommerce.gold`, but no SELECT. What happens to `SELECT * FROM ecommerce.gold.daily_sales`?
options: It fails — USE gives no permission on the data
It succeeds — USE SCHEMA implies SELECT on its tables
It returns column names but no rows
It succeeds only on a SQL warehouse
why: Correct.
Classic misconception: USE ≠ SELECT.
No partial result — the query is denied.
Warehouses enforce the same UC privileges.
exercises.explain: USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA only let you **traverse** the namespace. Data access needs `SELECT` on the table (or inherited from the schema/catalog). No compute type changes that.

exercises.q: Which set of grants is the minimum for group `analysts` to read `ecommerce.gold.daily_sales`?
options: USE CATALOG on `ecommerce` + USE SCHEMA on `ecommerce.gold` + SELECT on the table
exercises.explain: Three keys: building door (USE CATALOG), floor door (USE SCHEMA), room key (SELECT). ALL PRIVILEGES would work but violates least privilege.

exercises.q: Write the three GRANT statements so group `analysts` can run `SELECT * FROM ecommerce.gold.daily_sales;` — nothing more.
keywords: grant use catalog on catalog ecommerce
grant use schema on schema ecommerce.gold
exercises.explain: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are prerequisites; SELECT on the table grants the data. Granting SELECT at table level (not schema) is the least-privilege version.

exercises.q: These grants should let `analysts` read `ecommerce.gold.daily_sales`, but the query is denied. Find the buggy line.
lines: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG ecommerce TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA ecommerce.silver TO `analysts`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE ecommerce.gold.daily_sales TO `analysts`;
exercises.fix: GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA ecommerce.gold TO `analysts`;
exercises.explain: USE SCHEMA was granted on the **sibling** schema `silver`, not on `gold`. Without USE SCHEMA on the parent schema, the table can't be reached even with SELECT — Debugging Case 2.

exercises.q: A user has SELECT on `prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue` and USE CATALOG on `prod_ecommerce`, yet `SELECT * FROM prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue` returns PERMISSION_DENIED.

steps.prompt: The user swears "I have SELECT!". What do you check?

options.text: `SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold;` — is there USE SCHEMA for the user or their groups?
options.fb: Yes: SELECT is useless if you can't traverse the parent schema.

options.text: Re-grant SELECT on the table.
options.fb: SELECT is already there; repeating it changes nothing.

options.text: Restart the cluster.
options.fb: Compute restarts don't change UC privileges.

steps.prompt: No USE SCHEMA anywhere for them. Least-privilege fix?

options.text: `GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold TO` the user's group.
options.fb: Correct — that adds the missing prerequisite only.

options.text: `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold`.
options.fb: Works but grants far more than needed (MODIFY, CREATE …).

options.text: `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold`.
options.fb: SELECT on the schema still isn't USE SCHEMA; the traversal privilege is missing.

exercises.q: Case 2 — order your checks when a user has SELECT on a table but is denied.
items: Confirm the identity actually running the query
Check USE CATALOG on the parent catalog
Check USE SCHEMA on the exact parent schema
Confirm SELECT on the table (direct or inherited)
Grant only the missing prerequisite to the group
exercises.explain: Walk **top-down**: identity first, then the namespace prerequisites (catalog, schema), then the object privilege. Fix by adding only what's missing — usually `USE SCHEMA` — to a group.

exercises.q: (Interview) Explain the difference between USE SCHEMA and SELECT.
exercises.model: USE SCHEMA allows a principal to traverse/use the schema namespace, but it does not grant access to table data. To query a table, the user typically also needs USE CATALOG on the parent catalog and SELECT on the table or an inherited grant from the schema or catalog.
rubric: USE SCHEMA = traverse / use the namespace
SELECT on table or inherited parent grant
exercises.explain: The interview answer distinguishes **namespace traversal** (USE) from **data access** (SELECT) and names the full read path.

exercises.q: `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA ecommerce.gold TO analysts` was run last month (plus USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA). Today a new table `ecommerce.gold.churn` is created. Can analysts read it?
options: Yes — the schema-level SELECT is inherited by objects in the schema, including new ones
No — inheritance only covers tables that existed at grant time
Only if the new table is managed
exercises.explain: Inheritance flows from the schema to its children, so new tables are covered automatically. That's the power — and the risk — of hierarchical grants.

exercises.q: Schema `gold` has 2,000 tables. Three groups need read access. How many `GRANT SELECT` statements do you need if you grant at **schema** level and rely on inheritance?
exercises.explain: One schema-level grant per group = **3** (plus the USE prerequisites). Per table it would be 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 — exactly the grant sprawl Databricks tells you to avoid with inheritance.

exercises.q: Match each privilege to its meaning.
exercises.explain: SELECT reads, MODIFY is broad DML, finer-grained DML privileges such as INSERT (beta) narrow writes, USE SCHEMA only traverses.

exercises.q: Basic production model: who typically gets what on `prod.silver`?
exercises.explain: Analysts read (SELECT); engineers and especially pipeline service principals write (MODIFY or finer DML). Databricks recommends reserving direct writes in production for service principals.

exercises.q: Fill in the statements to inspect grants at every level.
exercises.explain: `SHOW GRANTS ON <type> <name>` answers "who has what?". Checking all three levels catches inherited grants.

exercises.q: Find the syntax bug in this revoke.
exercises.explain: GRANT … **TO** principal, but REVOKE … **FROM** principal. Using TO in a REVOKE is a syntax error.

exercises.q: Revoke group `analysts`' direct SELECT on `ecommerce.gold.daily_sales`, then show the grants on the schema to check for inherited access.
exercises.solution:
REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE ecommerce.gold.daily_sales FROM `analysts`;
SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA ecommerce.gold;
exercises.explain: After a REVOKE, always look **up** the hierarchy: a schema- or catalog-level SELECT keeps the access alive.

exercises.q: After `REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue FROM analysts`, members of analysts can no longer read that table.
exercises.explain: Not necessarily. If `SELECT` exists on schema `gold` or catalog `prod_ecommerce`, the table **inherits** it and access remains. Always inspect the hierarchy.

exercises.q: The admin revoked `SELECT ON TABLE prod_ecommerce.gold.daily_revenue FROM analysts`. An analyst still reads the table.

steps.prompt: First move?

options.text: `SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold;` and `SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG prod_ecommerce;`
options.fb: Yes — look for inherited SELECT above the table.

options.text: Run the REVOKE again.
options.fb: The direct grant is already gone; repeating it changes nothing.

options.text: Assume caching and wait an hour.
options.fb: Guessing. The usual cause is inheritance — verify it.

steps.prompt: You find `SELECT ON SCHEMA prod_ecommerce.gold TO analysts`. Goal: analysts read all gold tables EXCEPT daily_revenue. Best approach?

options.text: Remove the schema-level SELECT and grant SELECT on the specific gold tables they should read (or move daily_revenue to a schema they can't read).
options.fb: Right — inheritance can't be overridden by revoking at a lower level; restructure the grants.

options.text: Revoke at table level again, harder.
options.fb: A table-level REVOKE doesn't block a schema-level inherited grant.

options.text: Make the analysts owners of the table.
options.fb: That gives them more power, not less.

exercises.q: Case 3 — order your checks when access survives a REVOKE.
items: Confirm which principal/group the user reads through
SHOW GRANTS on the table (direct grant really gone?)
SHOW GRANTS on the parent schema (inherited SELECT?)
SHOW GRANTS on the parent catalog (inherited SELECT / ALL PRIVILEGES?)
Restructure grants at the right level
exercises.explain: Go bottom-up from the object you revoked: table → schema → catalog. Inherited grants higher up keep access alive; fix by restructuring where SELECT is granted.

exercises.q: Who should own the production table `prod.gold.revenue`?
why: Correct.
Personal ownership breaks when Nikos leaves.
Ownership is far more than reading — too much power.
Workspaces are not principals.
exercises.explain: Databricks recommends **groups** (or service principals) as owners of production objects. A personal owner disappears with the employee; analysts need SELECT, not ownership; a workspace can't own UC objects.

exercises.q: Which abilities does an object's owner typically have that a principal with only SELECT does not? (choose all)
options: Bypass row filters on every table in the metastore
exercises.explain: Owners can manage privileges, manage the object and transfer ownership. Ownership of one object doesn't grant powers across the whole metastore.

exercises.q: Transfer ownership of `prod.gold.revenue` from Nikos to the group `data_platform_admins`.
exercises.solution: ALTER TABLE prod.gold.revenue SET OWNER TO `data_platform_admins`;
exercises.explain: `ALTER <type> <name> [SET] OWNER TO principal` transfers ownership. Group ownership keeps production governance stable when people leave.

exercises.q: `ALL PRIVILEGES` includes `MANAGE`.
exercises.explain: False. Current UC docs exclude **MANAGE, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION and EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA** from ALL PRIVILEGES. A certification favourite.

exercises.q: Three of these are covered by `ALL PRIVILEGES` on a schema. Which one is not?
exercises.explain: MANAGE (delegated governance) is excluded from ALL PRIVILEGES, as are EXTERNAL USE LOCATION / EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA. Data and create privileges are included.

exercises.q: A platform team wants Maria to manage grants on schema `prod.gold` without making her (or anyone) the owner. Which privilege?
exercises.explain: **MANAGE** is the delegated-governance privilege: manage grants and ownership-related operations without being owner. ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE; BROWSE is discovery only; USE SCHEMA only traverses.

exercises.q: Why is `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON CATALOG prod_ecommerce TO all_company_users` a bad idea? Mention the dynamic evaluation.
exercises.model: It violates least privilege: every employee gets far more than they need (writes, creates, etc.) on all of production, which increases the blast radius of mistakes or compromised accounts. And ALL PRIVILEGES is evaluated dynamically: as new applicable privileges are added to the platform they are automatically included, so the grant silently grows over time. Databricks recommends restraint with ALL PRIVILEGES and MANAGE.
rubric: Violates least privilege / huge blast radius
Dynamic evaluation: future privileges included automatically
Restraint with ALL PRIVILEGES and MANAGE
exercises.explain: Two reasons: too broad today, and it grows tomorrow because ALL PRIVILEGES is evaluated dynamically.

exercises.q: You want every employee to discover which datasets exist in catalog `prod` (and request access), without reading any data. Which privilege?
exercises.explain: **BROWSE** gives metadata visibility/discoverability without data access. SELECT would expose data; MANAGE would let them change grants; USE CATALOG alone is a traversal prerequisite, not a discovery feature.

exercises.q: A principal with BROWSE on a catalog can run `SELECT *` on its tables.
exercises.explain: False. BROWSE shows that objects **exist** (metadata), not their data. To query, the user still requests and receives USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT.

exercises.q: "Managed" means the data is stored on Databricks' servers; "external" means it is stored in your cloud account.
exercises.explain: False. Both can be in **your** cloud object storage. The difference is **who controls the location and lifecycle** of the files: UC (managed) or you / an external system (external).

exercises.q: For an EXTERNAL table, who is responsible for what?

items.text: deleting files when no longer needed

exercises.explain: External tables still get full UC **governance** (metadata, permissions, lineage). Only **location + lifecycle** move to you. For managed tables UC does all five.

exercises.q: Complete the external table definition.
exercises.explain: `LOCATION` is what makes the table external: you specify the path. Omit it and UC picks a managed path.

exercises.q: `CREATE TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders (id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2));` — which kind of table is this, and who decides its storage path?
options: Managed — Unity Catalog decides the path (under the managed storage root)
External — the default bucket of the workspace
External — the path is the catalog name
Neither: a table without LOCATION is only a view
exercises.explain: No `LOCATION` → **managed** table; UC generates an internal location under the schema/catalog/metastore managed storage root.

exercises.q: You run `DROP TABLE ecommerce.silver.orders_ext;` on an EXTERNAL table. What happens?
options: UC metadata is removed; the files at the external path remain
Metadata and files are both deleted
Nothing — external tables can't be dropped
Files are deleted but metadata stays
why: Correct.
That's the managed behavior.
They can be dropped — only metadata goes.
Backwards.
exercises.explain: Dropping an **external** table removes the catalog entry only; the underlying files stay where you put them. For a **managed** table, UC also handles deleting the files.

exercises.q: A cleanup script. Which comment reveals a wrong assumption?
lines: -- orders_ext is an EXTERNAL table at s3://company-data/orders/
-- storage cost for s3://company-data/orders/ is now freed
-- recreate later with CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION if needed
exercises.fix: -- metadata removed; files at s3://company-data/orders/ remain → delete them with your storage tooling if truly unwanted
exercises.explain: Dropping an external table does **not** delete the files, so storage costs remain. (The last line is right: you can re-register the same path later.)

exercises.q: Managed or external? Classify each situation.

items.text: 10 TB of legacy Delta data already at known S3 paths
a non-Databricks system controls the files' lifecycle
migration constraints force data to stay at its path
a new gold aggregate for dashboards

exercises.explain: Default to managed for new Databricks workloads (automation, optimization, governance integration). External fits existing paths, external lifecycle control, migration constraints and interoperability.

exercises.q: Registering existing legacy Delta data as an external table — order the steps.
items: Delta data already exists at s3://company/legacy/orders/
An external location governs a path covering it
The principal holds the required privileges (e.g. CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location)
Run CREATE TABLE ecommerce.silver.legacy_orders USING DELTA LOCATION '…'
UC registers the metadata (data not rewritten)
exercises.explain: Data first, then governance of the path (external location), then privileges, then the CREATE TABLE … LOCATION, which only registers metadata.

exercises.q: `CREATE TABLE … USING DELTA LOCATION 's3://company/legacy/orders/'` on existing Delta data necessarily rewrites all the data files.
exercises.explain: False. Unity Catalog **registers metadata** pointing at the existing files; it does not necessarily rewrite them.

exercises.q: Register the existing Delta data at `s3://company/legacy/orders/` as table `ecommerce.silver.legacy_orders`.
exercises.explain: External table = CREATE TABLE … LOCATION. It works only if the path is under a governed external location and you have the privileges.

exercises.q: (Interview) What is the difference between a managed table and an external table in Unity Catalog?
exercises.model: Both are governed by Unity Catalog for metadata, access control, auditing and lineage. For a managed table, Unity Catalog additionally controls the underlying storage location and file lifecycle. For an external table, I provide the storage path and the underlying files remain externally managed; dropping the external table removes the catalog metadata but does not delete the underlying files.
rubric: Both: UC governance (metadata, access, auditing, lineage)
Managed: UC controls location + file lifecycle
External: I provide the path, lifecycle external
DROP external → metadata gone, files stay
exercises.explain: The strong answer starts with what is **the same** (governance) before the difference (location + lifecycle) and the DROP consequence.

exercises.q: Monday: a colleague says "I dropped `silver.orders_old` to save storage, but the S3 bill didn't change". Tuesday: another dropped `silver.orders_tmp` and "the data is gone from storage".

steps.prompt: What do you check for both tables?

options.text: Whether each was MANAGED or EXTERNAL (e.g. from the CREATE statement / DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED history or audit).
options.fb: Yes — DROP behavior depends entirely on the table type.

options.text: Whether the cluster was Photon-enabled.
options.fb: Compute engine doesn't decide DROP semantics.

options.text: Whether the user had SELECT.
options.fb: Both DROPs succeeded; this isn't a permission problem.

steps.prompt: `orders_old` was EXTERNAL. Explain the unchanged bill.

options.text: DROP removed only the UC metadata; the files at its LOCATION remain until someone deletes them with storage tooling.
options.fb: Correct — external lifecycle is your responsibility.

options.text: UC deletes external files after 30 days.
options.fb: UC doesn't manage external file lifecycle.

options.text: The DROP failed silently.
options.fb: The table entry is gone; the files were never UC's to delete.

steps.prompt: `orders_tmp` was MANAGED. Lesson for next time?

options.text: Check the type before DROP: a managed DROP lets UC delete the underlying files as part of its lifecycle.
options.fb: Right — managed = UC owns location and lifecycle.

options.text: Never use managed tables.
options.fb: Managed is the recommended default; just know the semantics.

options.text: Always add LOCATION so nothing is ever deleted.
options.fb: Making everything external pushes lifecycle work and governance gaps onto you.

exercises.q: Which managed storage location wins? Order from HIGHEST to LOWEST priority.
exercises.explain: The most specific (lowest-level) available location wins: schema, else catalog, else metastore. Databricks often recommends catalog-level storage as the isolation boundary.

exercises.q: Catalog `ecommerce` has MANAGED LOCATION `s3://uc/ecommerce/`; schema `ecommerce.finance` has MANAGED LOCATION `s3://uc/finance/`. A managed table is created in `ecommerce.finance`. Where do its files go?
options: Wherever the cluster's DBFS root is
exercises.explain: The **most specific** available managed location wins: the schema's. The catalog location would be used only if the schema had none.

exercises.q: Create catalog `ecommerce` whose managed tables are stored under `s3://company-uc/ecommerce/`.
exercises.explain: `MANAGED LOCATION` (not `LOCATION`) sets the catalog's managed storage root. It must be under an external location and you need CREATE MANAGED STORAGE.

exercises.q: `CREATE CATALOG ecommerce MANAGED LOCATION 's3://company-uc/ecommerce/'` fails. Which are plausible causes? (choose all)
options: The path is not under any Unity Catalog external location
You lack CREATE MANAGED STORAGE on the external location
You lack CREATE CATALOG on the metastore
The cluster has too few workers
exercises.explain: Managed locations must sit under an external location, need CREATE MANAGED STORAGE, and catalog creation itself needs CREATE CATALOG. Cluster size is irrelevant to authorization.

exercises.q: Match each cloud to what its storage credential typically wraps.
exercises.explain: A storage credential abstracts a **long-term cloud identity** so users never handle raw access keys.

exercises.q: What does an external location add that a storage credential alone doesn't have?
options: A specific cloud path (URI) bound to the credential, as a securable boundary
A cloud identity to authenticate with
exercises.explain: The credential says **who** (which cloud identity). The external location says **where** (which path) + which credential, and it's a securable you grant on.

exercises.q: Complete the external location definition.
exercises.explain: `CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION name URL '<path>' WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL <cred>)` binds a path to a credential.

exercises.q: Order the chain from cloud identity down to the files.
exercises.explain: Cloud identity → credential (UC abstraction) → external location (path + credential) → table/volume metadata → the actual files.

exercises.q: Why does Databricks recommend granting `CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE` on an external location instead of on the storage credential?
options: It scopes the permission to a specific path — path-scoped least privilege
exercises.explain: A credential may reach a huge storage scope; an external location like `s3://company/finance/` limits access to that path. Credentials **are** securables — the point is granularity.

exercises.q: Allow group `data_engineers` to create external tables only under the external location `finance_loc`.
exercises.explain: Granting on the external location (not the credential) scopes the privilege to its path.

exercises.q: One storage credential can be used by several external locations, each with its own UC access boundary.
exercises.explain: True. E.g. credential A backs `s3://company/raw/`, `.../archive/` and `.../shared/`, and each location gets separate grants.

exercises.q: "External location" and "external table" are synonyms.
exercises.explain: False. An **external location** is a governed storage **path** (+ credential). An **external table** is **table metadata** pointing at tabular data **inside** such a governed path.

exercises.q: (Interview) Storage credential vs external location?
exercises.model: A storage credential represents the cloud identity Databricks can use to authenticate to object storage (an IAM role, managed identity or service account). An external location binds that credential to a specific governed cloud-storage URI, giving Unity Catalog a securable path boundary on which privileges can be granted. One credential can back many external locations.
rubric: Location is a securable path boundary
exercises.explain: Identity (credential) vs path-scoped securable (location).

exercises.q: `SELECT * FROM prod.silver.orders` (managed) works. `SELECT * FROM prod.silver.legacy_orders` (external at s3://company/legacy/orders/) fails with a storage access error.

steps.prompt: You already confirmed USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on both tables. Where next?

options.text: The extra external-storage layers: external location, storage credential, workspace binding, cloud IAM.
options.fb: Right — the managed table proves the UC grants work; the difference is the storage path.

options.text: Re-grant SELECT on the external table.
options.fb: SELECT is already fine; the managed one works with the same grants.

options.text: Switch to a bigger cluster.
options.fb: Sizing doesn't cause storage access errors.

steps.prompt: Which external-location question first?

options.text: Is `s3://company/legacy/orders/` covered by an external location, and is it bound to this workspace?
options.fb: Yes — no governed path, or a location not usable in this workspace, means no access.

options.text: Is the table partitioned?
options.fb: Partitioning doesn't affect authorization.

options.text: Does the table have a column mask?
options.fb: Masks change values, they don't cause storage access errors.

steps.prompt: Location exists and is bound. The cloud team rotated the IAM role's policy last night. Fix?

options.text: Have the cloud team restore read access for the IAM role behind the storage credential to that path.
options.fb: Correct — UC can't grant what the cloud identity itself is not allowed to do.

options.text: Give the users AWS access keys.
options.fb: Bypasses governance — exactly what storage credentials exist to avoid.

options.text: Convert the table to managed by DROP + CREATE.
options.fb: Drastic and doesn't fix the broken credential.

exercises.q: Case 4 — order the extra checks for an external table that fails while managed tables work.
items: Confirm UC grants (USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA / SELECT) — managed works, so likely fine
Find the table's LOCATION (DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED)
Check the external location covering that path + privileges on it
Check workspace binding of the external location / credential
Check the storage credential and the cloud IAM permissions behind it
exercises.explain: Start from what's proven (UC grants), then follow the storage chain outward: location → external location → binding → credential → cloud IAM.

exercises.q: Table or volume?

items.text: daily order rows queried with SQL
JSON config files for a job

exercises.explain: Tables are for rows/columns with SQL/DataFrame semantics and Delta history. Volumes govern non-tabular or raw files — PDFs, images, configs, landing files.

exercises.q: Complete the statements: a managed volume, then an external one.
exercises.explain: `CREATE VOLUME` = managed (UC picks the location). `CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME … LOCATION` = you specify the path.

exercises.q: Dropping an external volume deletes the files at its LOCATION.
exercises.explain: False. As with external tables: metadata is removed, **underlying files remain**. A managed volume drop can remove the data as part of the managed lifecycle.

exercises.q: Which set lets `data_scientists` READ files in volume `ecommerce.raw.documents`?
options: USE CATALOG ecommerce + USE SCHEMA ecommerce.raw + READ VOLUME on the volume
exercises.explain: Volumes use **READ VOLUME / WRITE VOLUME**, plus the usual USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA prerequisites. SELECT is a table privilege.

exercises.q: Match the action to the privilege it needs (beyond USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA).
exercises.explain: Tables: SELECT / MODIFY. Volumes: READ VOLUME / WRITE VOLUME. Table and volume permissions are **not** identical.

exercises.q: Grant group `data_scientists` read access to files in volume `ecommerce.raw.documents` (assume they already have the USE privileges).
exercises.explain: Object type keyword is `VOLUME`; the privilege is `READ VOLUME`.

exercises.q: This code should read a JSON file from volume `documents` in schema `raw` of catalog `ecommerce`. Which line is wrong?
lines: # read config from the governed volume
exercises.explain: Volume paths follow the namespace order: `/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/<file>`. Swapping catalog and schema points at a non-existent volume.

exercises.q: Which is the recommended way to reach a non-tabular file governed by UC?
options: Copy it into a Delta table first
exercises.explain: Databricks recommends **/Volumes/...** paths for direct non-tabular file access (governed file-path semantics) and table names for tables — not raw cloud URIs scattered through code.

exercises.q: A volume gives you Delta table history (DESCRIBE HISTORY) for its files.
exercises.explain: False. Delta table history is a **table** feature. Volumes govern files; they don't give table semantics or history.

exercises.q: A user with USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA runs `open("/Volumes/ecommerce/raw/documents/file.json")` and it fails.

steps.prompt: What's the first privilege to check?

options.text: READ VOLUME on `ecommerce.raw.documents`.
options.fb: Yes — USE privileges are prerequisites; READ VOLUME opens the files.

options.text: SELECT on the schema.
options.fb: SELECT is a table privilege; it doesn't open volumes.

options.text: MODIFY on the volume.
options.fb: MODIFY is for tables; volumes use READ/WRITE VOLUME.

steps.prompt: Granted READ VOLUME; reading works. Now the user's job writes `open(path, "w")` and fails. Next?

options.text: Grant WRITE VOLUME as well (READ + WRITE VOLUME for writes).
options.fb: Correct — writes need WRITE VOLUME on top of the read set.

options.text: Grant ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog.
options.fb: Massive over-grant for one write.

options.text: Make it an external volume.
options.fb: Volume type doesn't remove the need for WRITE VOLUME.

exercises.q: Case 5 — order the checks for a failing /Volumes/ file access.
items: WRITE VOLUME too, if it's a write
External volume? then external location / credential / IAM
exercises.explain: Path first (cheapest), then the namespace prerequisites, then the volume privileges, and the storage layers only for external volumes.

exercises.q: (Interview) Volume vs table?
exercises.model: A table provides structured relational semantics over rows and columns, while a Unity Catalog volume provides governed access to non-tabular files in cloud storage. Tables use privileges such as SELECT and MODIFY, whereas volumes use READ VOLUME and WRITE VOLUME. Files in volumes are accessed through /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/ paths.
exercises.explain: Name the semantics difference and the privilege difference.

exercises.q: Which UC objects can be restricted with workspace bindings (per the source)? (choose all)
exercises.explain: Workspace bindings apply to **catalogs, external locations and storage credentials**. Column-level control is done with masks/ABAC, not bindings.

exercises.q: If a user holds USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on `prod.finance.payroll`, the query must succeed from any workspace attached to the metastore.
exercises.explain: False. A **workspace binding** can restrict `prod` to specific workspaces. User privileges are not the only authorization boundary.

exercises.q: Nikos has USE CATALOG prod, USE SCHEMA prod.finance and SELECT on prod.finance.payroll. From `dev-workspace` the query fails; his teammate in `prod-workspace` runs the same query fine.

steps.prompt: Grants are identical for both (same group). What's the strongest hypothesis?

options.text: Catalog `prod` is bound only to `prod-workspace`.
options.fb: Yes — same principal grants, different workspace → binding.

options.text: Nikos lacks SELECT.
options.fb: Same group, same grants; the teammate succeeds.

options.text: The table is external.
options.fb: Then it would fail in both workspaces.

steps.prompt: Binding confirmed. What's the right fix?

options.text: Run it from prod-workspace, or — if dev access is truly intended — have an admin add a binding for dev-workspace.
options.fb: Bindings are deliberate isolation; change them only if the design allows it.

options.text: Grant ALL PRIVILEGES on prod to Nikos.
options.fb: Grants can't override a missing workspace binding.

options.text: Copy payroll into the dev catalog.
options.fb: That copies sensitive data around and defeats the isolation.

exercises.q: Order the checks when grants look correct but a catalog is unreachable from your workspace.
items: Confirm USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA / SELECT
Check which workspace you are in
Retry from a bound workspace or request a binding change
exercises.explain: Identity and grants first (the common causes), then the separate workspace-binding boundary.

exercises.q: Which compute can access Unity Catalog? (choose all)
options: Classic compute with Standard access mode
Classic compute with Dedicated access mode
A legacy cluster configuration that isn't UC-compatible
exercises.explain: Standard and Dedicated classic compute, serverless and Databricks SQL support UC. A legacy/non-UC configuration fails even with perfect grants.

exercises.q: If all Unity Catalog permissions are correct, the query succeeds on any cluster.
exercises.explain: False. **permissions correct + wrong legacy compute = still failure.** Compute must be UC-compatible.

exercises.q: A notebook on an old team cluster fails to read `prod.silver.orders`; the same user reads it fine from a SQL warehouse.

steps.prompt: Grants are the same in both cases. Which layer differs?

options.text: Compute: the old cluster may not be UC-compatible.
options.fb: Same principal + same grants + different compute → compute layer.

options.text: The table's row filter.
options.fb: Row filters apply regardless of compute; they wouldn't cause a fail-vs-success split here.

options.text: USE SCHEMA.
options.fb: Then the warehouse query would fail too.

steps.prompt: Fix?

options.text: Use a cluster with Standard (or Dedicated) access mode, or serverless.
options.fb: Correct — UC-compatible compute.

options.text: Grant SELECT again.
options.fb: Grants are already fine.

options.text: Add more workers.
options.fb: Size doesn't make a cluster UC-compatible.

exercises.q: Order the checks when the same user and grants work on a SQL warehouse but fail on a cluster.
items: Confirm identity and grants are identical in both runs
Re-run the query on serverless / a SQL warehouse to isolate compute
Switch to Standard/Dedicated access mode or serverless
exercises.explain: Same principal + same grants + different compute isolates the compute layer; UC needs Standard/Dedicated, serverless or Databricks SQL.

exercises.q: What does a row filter do?
options: A SQL UDF evaluated at query time; rows where it returns false are removed from the result
A job that deletes forbidden rows from the table files
A view the user must query instead of the table
A cluster setting that hides partitions
exercises.explain: Row filters are **query-time** policies — stored data is untouched; different users see different rows of the same table.

exercises.q: Attach the row filter to the table.
exercises.explain: `ALTER TABLE … SET ROW FILTER <function> ON (<column>)` binds the UDF; the listed column is passed as the function's argument.

exercises.q: With the `country_filter` from the lesson, table `sales` has 100 GR, 80 DE and 20 FR rows. How many rows does a member of `greece_sales` (and NOT of `global_sales`) see with `SELECT *`?
exercises.explain: The function returns TRUE for global_sales (no), then for greece_sales AND country='GR' → only the **100** GR rows; DE and FR rows hit ELSE FALSE and are removed.

exercises.q: Write a row filter function `security.country_filter(country STRING)` that returns TRUE for members of `global_sales`, TRUE for `greece_sales` members on GR rows, otherwise FALSE — and attach it to `ecommerce.gold.sales` on column `country`.
exercises.solution:
CREATE FUNCTION security.country_filter(country STRING)
RETURN
  CASE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('global_sales') THEN TRUE
    WHEN is_account_group_member('greece_sales') AND country = 'GR' THEN TRUE
    ELSE FALSE
  END;

ALTER TABLE ecommerce.gold.sales
SET ROW FILTER security.country_filter
ON (country);
exercises.explain: A filter UDF returns a boolean per row; `is_account_group_member` makes it user-aware. Default FALSE is the safe choice.

exercises.q: This filter should show GR rows to greece_sales and everything to global_sales. Which line makes it leak data?
lines: WHEN is_account_group_member('greece_sales') AND country = 'GR' THEN TRUE
exercises.explain: `ELSE TRUE` shows every row to everyone not matched above — the filter filters nothing. Default must be **FALSE** (deny by default).

exercises.q: A column mask changes the value stored in the Delta files for users without privilege.
exercises.explain: False. The stored value (e.g. 5000) is unchanged; the mask is a **query-time** policy, so finance_admin sees 5000 and an analyst sees **** / NULL / a bucket.

exercises.q: Attach the mask function to the salary column.
exercises.text:
ALTER TABLE ecommerce.gold.employees
[[ALTER COLUMN]] salary SET [[MASK]] security.mask_salary;
exercises.explain: Masks are set per column: `ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN <col> SET MASK <function>`.

exercises.q: You have 10,000 tables and want every column tagged `sensitivity = pii` masked for users without privilege — including tables created next month. Best tool?
options: ABAC: governed tags + a central policy
A column mask attached manually to each table
A row filter on each table
exercises.explain: ABAC scales: tag the data, write one policy; a new tagged table tomorrow is **automatically covered**. Manual per-table masks don't scale and are easy to forget.

exercises.q: Per-table policy or ABAC?

items.text: one table with unique country logic
mask every PII-tagged column across the lakehouse
new tagged tables must be covered automatically
a special salary rule for one HR table
consistent policy enforcement across thousands of tables

exercises.explain: Databricks recommends ABAC for consistent enforcement across many tables; direct filters/masks fit per-table logic.

exercises.q: ABAC can apply row filters and column masks, and now also policy-based GRANT/DENY capabilities in supported scopes.
exercises.explain: True per the source: ABAC policies cover row filters, column masks and policy-based GRANT/DENY in supported scopes.

exercises.q: An analyst says: "I have SELECT on `ecommerce.gold.employees`, but salary shows `****`. Fix my permissions!"

steps.prompt: What do you tell yourself first?

options.text: SELECT ≠ unfiltered raw visibility — look for fine-grained policies.
options.fb: Right: the query succeeded, so grants are fine; a policy changed the values.

options.text: Grant MODIFY so they can see real values.
options.fb: MODIFY is write access and doesn't bypass masks.

options.text: The data is corrupted.
options.fb: Stored values are intact; masking is query-time.

steps.prompt: Where do you look?

options.text: Column mask on `salary`, row filter on the table, and any ABAC policy matching tags on the column.
options.fb: Those three change visibility.

options.text: SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG only.
options.fb: Grants don't explain masked values.

options.text: The cluster's Spark config.
options.fb: Masks are UC policies, not Spark settings.

steps.prompt: A mask returns real salary only to `finance_admins`. The analyst isn't in it. Correct outcome?

options.text: Working as designed; if the business approves, add them to the right group — don't remove the mask.
options.fb: The policy is doing its job; access changes go through group membership.

options.text: Drop the mask for everyone.
options.fb: That exposes salary to all readers.

options.text: Give the analyst ownership.
options.fb: Ownership is not a way around governance.

exercises.q: Case 6 — order the checks for "query works but values are masked / rows missing".
items: Confirm the query succeeded (so base grants are fine)
Check for a column mask on the column
Check for a row filter on the table
Check the user's group memberships used by the policy functions
exercises.explain: A successful query rules out missing grants. Then inspect the fine-grained layers and the group memberships those policies test.

exercises.q: Which statements about UC lineage are true per the source? (choose all)
options: Collected automatically for queries run on Databricks
Can go down to column level
Aggregated across workspaces sharing the same metastore
Must be declared manually in a YAML file
exercises.explain: Lineage is automatic, column-level and metastore-wide. No manual declaration is needed.

exercises.q: Before renaming `silver.orders.customer_id`, what should you do?
options: Check its column-level lineage to find downstream tables, dashboards, features and reports
Just run ALTER — Delta keeps history
Grant MODIFY to everyone so they can fix their code
exercises.explain: Lineage enables **impact analysis**: see `customer_id → gold.customer_360 → executive_dashboard` before breaking it. Time travel doesn't fix broken consumers.

exercises.q: Dashboard revenue is wrong. Order the upstream walk.
exercises.explain: Walk upstream along lineage from the symptom; the first layer where the value is already wrong is where the bug was introduced (it's in the transformation into that layer).

exercises.q: The executive dashboard shows revenue 3× too high for yesterday.

steps.prompt: First step?

options.text: Open lineage for the dashboard to find its upstream table(s).
options.fb: Lineage gives you the path to walk.

options.text: Re-run every pipeline.
options.fb: Re-running hides the evidence and may repeat the bug.

options.text: Grant analysts MODIFY to fix the numbers.
options.fb: Never patch outputs by hand.

steps.prompt: gold.daily_revenue is 3× too high; silver.orders looks correct. Conclusion?

options.text: The bug was introduced in the silver → gold transformation (e.g. a bad join duplicating rows).
options.fb: First layer where the value is wrong = the transformation just before it.

options.text: Bronze ingestion is broken.

exercises.q: Order the 8 layers of the permission-debugging algorithm.

exercises.q: In your own words: what does "think the whole authorization chain, not just SELECT" mean?
exercises.model: A permission error can come from any layer: the wrong executing identity (job run-as), a workspace binding, missing USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA, the object privilege itself (or an inherited grant), fine-grained policies (row filters, column masks, ABAC), the external storage chain (external location, credential, cloud IAM), or non-UC-compatible compute. So I walk the layers in order instead of assuming SELECT is missing or asking for admin.
exercises.explain: The Phase-3 outcome: a permission error is a chain, and you walk it in order.

exercises.q: Q1. What is the top-level Unity Catalog object?
exercises.explain: The **metastore** is the top-level UC container for metadata and permissions. Catalogs live inside it; workspaces and accounts aren't UC namespace objects.

exercises.q: Q2. What does `prod.finance.payroll` mean?
exercises.explain: Three-level namespace: catalog.schema.object.

exercises.q: Q3. The workspace is above the catalog in the Unity Catalog namespace.
exercises.explain: No. The workspace is an operational environment; the catalog lives inside a UC **metastore**.

exercises.q: Q4. Multiple workspaces can use one metastore.
exercises.explain: Yes — typically within the same regional metastore architecture, subject to workspace bindings and permissions.

exercises.q: Q5. What is a securable object?
options: A Unity Catalog object on which privileges can be granted to principals
A user, group or service principal
A cluster with Dedicated access mode
exercises.explain: Securable = UC object you can grant on. The principal is the WHO; encryption and clusters are unrelated.

exercises.q: Q6. A principal receives permissions. Which one is NOT a principal?
exercises.explain: Principals are users, groups and service principals. A schema is a **securable**.

exercises.q: Q7. USE CATALOG lets me SELECT every table in the catalog.
exercises.explain: No. It's only a traversal prerequisite.

exercises.q: Q8. The typical read path — order the grants from outermost to innermost.
exercises.explain: Catalog → schema → object.

exercises.q: Q9. Why are groups preferred to individual grants?
options: They centralize membership management and reduce permission sprawl
exercises.explain: One grant per group, membership changes instead of grant changes. Users **can** receive grants — it just doesn't scale.

exercises.q: Q10. Why use service principals for production pipelines?
options: Stable machine identity, decoupled from individual employee lifecycle
exercises.explain: If an employee leaves, a personal-identity pipeline breaks; an SP doesn't. SPs are fully subject to UC grants.

exercises.q: Q11. What is ownership?
options: An administrative/control relationship with an object, including broad management and grant-delegation capabilities
The workspace where the object was created
exercises.explain: Owners can manage the object, manage privileges and transfer ownership — far more than SELECT.

exercises.q: Q12. Is ALL PRIVILEGES literally every possible privilege? Which are excluded? (choose all)
exercises.explain: No — MANAGE, EXTERNAL USE LOCATION and EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA are excluded.

exercises.q: Q13. Managed vs external: who controls the storage lifecycle?
buckets: UC governance only; you/external system control lifecycle
exercises.explain: Managed → UC owns location and lifecycle. External → UC governs, you control location and lifecycle.

exercises.q: Q14. Dropping an external table deletes its files.
exercises.explain: No. Underlying files remain; only UC metadata is removed.

exercises.q: Q15. What happens to the files when you drop a MANAGED table?
options: Unity Catalog manages their deletion as part of the managed lifecycle
They move to the external location
exercises.explain: For managed tables UC owns the file lifecycle, including deletion after DROP.

exercises.q: Q16–Q18. Match each question to its answer.
pairs: governed abstraction of a cloud authentication identity
cloud path + storage credential, as a securable
Why grant on an external location, not the raw credential?
exercises.explain: Credential = identity, location = path + identity, grants on location = path-scoped least privilege.

exercises.q: Q19. What is a volume?
options: A Unity Catalog governed container for non-tabular files
A disk attached to the driver
exercises.explain: Volumes govern files (PDFs, images, raw files) with /Volumes/... paths.

exercises.q: Q20. Volume read privileges?
exercises.explain: Same prerequisites as tables, but the object privilege is READ VOLUME.

exercises.q: Q21. Table permissions and volume permissions are identical.
exercises.explain: No. Tables use e.g. SELECT, MODIFY; volumes use READ VOLUME, WRITE VOLUME.

exercises.q: Q22. What is a workspace binding?
options: A restriction specifying which workspaces can access certain UC objects (catalogs, external locations, storage credentials)
Attaching a notebook to a cluster
The link between an account and its billing
A grant from a workspace admin to a user
exercises.explain: Bindings restrict where (from which workspaces) catalogs, external locations and credentials can be used — independent of user grants.

exercises.q: Q28. Unity Catalog captures column-level lineage.
exercises.explain: Yes, for supported Databricks queries/workloads.

exercises.q: Q29. Fill in the likely debugging sequence for PERMISSION_DENIED.
exercises.text: actual [[principal]] → workspace [[binding]] → USE CATALOG → USE SCHEMA → object [[privilege]] → [[fine-grained]] policies → storage/external location → [[compute]] compatibility
exercises.explain: Identity, binding, catalog, schema, object, fine-grained, storage, compute — I Bet Cats Sit On Fluffy Silk Cushions.

exercises.q: Q30. Why can a job fail although your notebook succeeds?
options: The job may execute as a different service principal with different UC privileges
Jobs can only read managed tables
exercises.explain: Different executor, different grants — Case 1 of the algorithm.
